title: Milestones and trends: the role of the fossil record in reconstructing plant evolution – an introduction to the Special Issue
content: For over two centuries, palaeobotanists have studied a myriad of plant fossils with no end in sight given the steady stream of new fossil discoveries. Annals of Botany has been an important contributor to this pattern from its very beginnings, with a first palaeobotany paper published in 1888, the second year of the journal’s existence, by none other than William C. Williamson, one of the founders of palaeobotany as a scientific discipline (Williamson, 1888). Following that auspicious beginning, the list of scientists who published on fossil plants in the journal’s first five decades reads like a who’s who of botany, including Albert C. Seward, David P. Penhallow, Dunkinfield H. Scott, Agnes Arber, Francis W. Oliver, Hermann Graf zu Solms-Laubach, Marie Stopes, Edward C. Jeffrey, Margaret J. Benson, John Walton, Suzanne Leclercq, Charles E. Bertrand, Edward W. Berry, Ruth Holden, Birbal Sahni, William H. Lang and Wilfred N. Edwards. This work cemented Annals of Botany as a leader in palaeobotanical research, a legacy that we are pleased to see still in place today. This Special Issue showcases the current state of palaeobotanical research almost 140 years after the first palaeobotanical publication in Annals of Botany and demonstrates the active role that fossils continue to play for our understanding of plant evolution.
